extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, advertisers, propagandists, political operatives
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and executing modern propaganda/public-relations campaigns: how to shape events, choose media, enlist authorities, and ethically present information to influence public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscious and intelligent manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: “The conscious and intelligent manipulation of the organized habits and opinions of the masses” (Bernays' definition of the core activity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propaganda should be purposeful, planned and informed by an understanding of mass mental processes; avoid accidental or purely ad-hoc appeals. This is the fundamental operative principle: act deliberately to shape habits and opinions rather than rely on chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda as consistent, enduring effort
rubrics_metrics.description: “Modern propaganda is a consistent, enduring effort to create or shape events to influence the relations of the public to an enterprise, idea or group.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Campaigns should be sustained over time and designed to create or shape circumstances (not merely one-off ads). Short impulsive pushes are less effective than continuous, strategic activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit of cause and correctness of information (ethical standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether propaganda is good or bad “depends upon the merit of the cause urged, and the correctness of the information published.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propaganda becomes reprehensible when authors knowingly disseminate lies or aim for effects prejudicial to the common good. Accuracy, candor and consideration of public welfare are ethical constraints on practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create or shape events / manufacture newsworthy circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: The propagandist should "create circumstances" and "create pictures in the minds of millions"—i.e., generate events or situations that have news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than attempting to 'contaminate' editorial content, public relations counsel should create real events or occurrences that editors will consider newsworthy. Example: organizing a fashion service in Paris to generate genuine fashion events that media then report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target the anatomy of society and interlocking groups
rubrics_metrics.description: The new technique "takes account...of the anatomy of society, with its interlocking group formations" and treats the individual as a cell in social units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map social cleavages (professional, religious, racial, trade groups) and plan appeals to specific groups and the channels they use. Touch "sensitive spots" in groups to elicit automatic responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlist key leaders / opinion authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Use "key men in every group—persons whose mere word carried authority to hundreds or thousands of followers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and recruit influential leaders (editors, clergy, trade leaders, fashion authorities) whose endorsement will cascade through multiple group memberships. Leverage their credibility rather than address the mass directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit media shifts and choose appropriate instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: The relative value of instruments of propaganda (newspapers, radio, motion pictures, lectures, etc.) is constantly changing; the propagandist must take advantage of these shifts the instant they occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuously monitor media landscape; adapt tactics to emerging dominant channels (e.g., radio, film, automobiles in Bernays' era). Use the medium whose reach and form best match the intended audience and message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the message newsworthy (news value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors publish what they deem to have "news value"; if a public-relations counsel can breathe life into an idea and make it one of the day's events, it will receive attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame and stage activities so they compete successfully in editorial selection. Ensure events have timeliness, significance, prominence, or human interest to qualify as news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source clarity and factual accuracy for news items
rubrics_metrics.description: “The source of the news offered to the editor should always be clearly stated and the facts accurately presented.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When pitching to media, disclose provenance and ensure factual correctness to maintain credibility and avoid being dismissed. Transparency about sources increases editorial acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor approach to media type (newspapers vs. magazines vs. radio vs. film)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different media have different roles: newspapers prioritize day-to-day news; magazines select material in line with a continuous policy; radio reaches masses simultaneously; motion pictures standardize ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Customize content format and strategy to each medium: pitch timely events to newspapers, serialized or thematic material to magazines, mass-simultaneous appeals to radio, and broad cultural narratives to film.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use repetition to accustom public to change
rubrics_metrics.description: Propaganda, by repeatedly interpreting new scientific ideas and inventions to the public, has made the public more receptive—it 'is accustoming the public to change and progress.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ repeated exposures across channels to normalize new concepts or products; single mentions rarely shift mass opinion. Plan frequency and reinforcement across platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage personalities carefully and authentically
rubrics_metrics.description: Personality is an instrument of propaganda; the public instinctively demands a personality to typify enterprises. Present an outward picture "consistent with his real character and his aims."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop, manage, and protect public personalities; avoid absurd or inauthentic portrayals that can backfire. Treat personality as an objective asset to be aligned with campaign goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate expert/technical content into intelligible public messages
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions (museums, science labs) must "study how best to make [their] message intelligible to the community" and interpret models of beauty or scientific discovery for public understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplify and contextualize technical or aesthetic content so lay audiences can grasp its meaning and value. Educational offers to schools should be judged on educational merits and candor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work at the source/influencers of trends (e.g., fashion houses)
rubrics_metrics.description: To change fashion, Bernays' velvet example shows attacking the source—Paris couturiers and manufactories—then leveraging editors and department stores to propagate the style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Influence upstream authorities or originators of trends rather than only downstream consumers; stage endorsements and authentic usage to trigger media echo and consumer adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous and systematic employment by intelligent minorities
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is the intelligent minorities which need to make use of propaganda continuously and systematically" because small groups can make the rest of society think as they wish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design long-term programs with consistent messaging and organizational persistence; episodic campaigns are less effective in shaping durable public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect changing social organization and multiple affiliations
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals belong to many interlacing groups (church, club, profession) and will disseminate opinions from one group to another; propaganda must recognize these interlocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan multi-group diffusion strategies: seed messages in one affiliation with awareness of cross-membership pathways to amplify reach and influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deliberate deceit and harmful aims (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propaganda becomes vicious when its authors "consciously and deliberately disseminate what they know to be lies, or when they aim at effects which they know to be prejudicial to the common good."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not fabricate facts or knowingly pursue actions that harm public welfare. Ethical limits both protect publics and preserve long-term efficacy and credibility of campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make use of all available communication means (omnichannel)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no means of human communication which may not also be a means of deliberate propaganda; the propagandist must be alert to all channels (press, radio, motion pictures, lectures, schools, personalities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt an omnichannel mindset—identify every plausible route to audience contact and coordinate messages across them for cumulative effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage institutional authority and organizational endorsements
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements or reports released by authoritative institutions (State Department, Carnegie Foundation, presidents of boards) carry weight and are accepted by the public as authoritative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secure institutional backing or reputable spokespersons to lend credibility; use institutional releases strategically to frame public understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure acceptability by editorial independence and audience relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors decide publication based on news value and public interest; newspapers strive for accuracy and interest to large groups rather than serving as guarantees against partisan benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing material for press, evaluate how it meets editorial criteria—accuracy, significance, and audience relevance—rather than expecting sympathetic placement due to sponsor's interests.
